01.event: While Rav Hamnuna studied before Ulla, Ulla praised him but lamented that he came from Harpanya, a town of flawed lineage.
01.turn: Rav Hamnuna was ashamed; Ulla asked where he paid his poll tax and learned it was Pum Nahara.
01.outcome: Ulla declared that he was therefore from Pum Nahara, clearing his lineage.
01.summary: Rav Hamnuna was studying before Ulla, who exclaimed what a great man he was, if only he were not from Harpanya, a town known for flawed lineage. Rav Hamnuna was embarrassed. Ulla asked him where he paid his poll tax, and he answered Pum Nahara. Ulla concluded that he was then really from Pum Nahara, and his lineage was sound.

02.event: A case about an alleyway closed by the sea on one side and a garbage dump on the other came before Rabbi.
02.turn: Rabbi declined to rule either way.
02.outcome: He said neither prohibition nor permission.
02.summary: There was an alleyway with the sea at one end and a garbage dump at the other, and the question of whether one could carry in it came before Rabbi. He gave no ruling at all, neither forbidding nor permitting it.
02.missing: Any reaction or consequence of the non-ruling; the reasoning given afterward is commentary, not narrative.

03.actor: A man in Mata Mehasya and his brother
03.event: A man's brother tried to disqualify the man's yevama by giving her a bill of divorce, fearing being cheated over the dead brother's property.
03.turn: The man offered to divide the property, and when the brother feared a swindle like the one in Pumbedita, offered to let him take his share immediately.
03.summary: A man in Mata Mehasya was due to marry his late brother's widow, but another brother wanted to disqualify her with a bill of divorce. The man asked why, offering to share the estate. The brother said he feared being cheated as the Pumbedita swindler had cheated his brother, so the man offered to let him take his share right away.
03.missing: How the dispute ended; the passage moves into legal discussion of the offer.

05.event: Walking on the road with a woman ahead of them, Rav urged Rav Yehuda to hurry away from her.
05.turn: Rav Yehuda cited Rav's own ruling that men of good morals may be together with a woman; Rav said that did not mean the two of them.
05.outcome: Rav explained it applied only to people like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues.
05.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were walking along a road with a woman ahead of them. Rav told Rav Yehuda to quicken his steps away from Gehenna. Rav Yehuda objected that Rav himself had permitted this for men of good character, but Rav replied that he had not meant men like them, only men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues.

06.actor: Rabba bar Avuh and Rav Nahman
06.event: Rabba bar Avuh told the Sages to examine Rav Nahman in the bath, and if his flesh gave off steam he would give him his daughter.
06.summary: Rabba bar Avuh instructed the Sages to watch Rav Nahman while he bathed, promising that if his body gave off steam (showing he was not impotent) he would give him his daughter in marriage.
06.missing: Whether the examination happened and what came of it; the passage cites the instruction only for a legal point.

07.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with beer sediment belonging to his employer.
07.turn: The owner found him and asked why he had not used the better sediment, and the brewer asked Rava whether this meant consent.
07.outcome: Rava ruled that such a remark counts as consent only for teruma, so the brewer had no right to the sediment.
07.summary: A brewer making beer for someone betrothed a woman with some of the beer's sediment. The owner found him and asked why he had not used the better, sharper sediment instead. The brewer asked Rava whether this showed the owner's consent, making the betrothal valid. Rava said that remark signals consent only in matters of teruma, not here.

08.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged in the street by a pig.
08.turn: He exclaimed that a mouth that produced pearls should not lick dust.
08.summary: According to one account, Elisha ben Avuya, known as Aher, saw the tongue of the executed scholar Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged along by a pig. Appalled, he cried out that a mouth which had produced pearls should not lick the dust. Because of this he went out and abandoned the path, sinning.

09.actor: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin (or Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Zevida), and Ameimar
09.event: A visiting sage ruled on the offspring of a slave and a Jewish woman in Rav Gazza's town.
09.turn: Reports conflict over who the sage was and whether he declared the offspring of a married woman unfit.
09.outcome: Another report says Ameimar visited and declared the offspring fit in both cases.
09.summary: Rav Gazza reported that a visiting sage came to his town and ruled on two cases of children born to Jewish women from slaves: fit if the mother was unmarried, unfit if married. Another version says the sage was a different Rabbi Yosei who declared both fit. Separately, Ameimar visited another town and also declared the offspring fit in both cases.
09.missing: Any turn beyond the rulings themselves; these are reports of decisions rather than a developed narrative.

11.actor: Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Elazar and Reish Lakish
11.event: Rabbi Yohanan taught a ruling about burning notar and Rabbi Elazar refuted him from a baraita.
11.turn: Rabbi Yohanan, silenced, praised Rabbi Elazar as expounding like Moses, but Reish Lakish revealed it was a baraita from Torat Kohanim.
11.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan went and learned Torat Kohanim in three days and mastered it in three months.
11.summary: Rabbi Yohanan was teaching that leftover sacrificial meat burned after its time may be burned at night. Rabbi Elazar challenged him with a teaching that the verse extends the daytime requirement, and Rabbi Yohanan fell silent. Afterward he told Reish Lakish he had seen ben Pedat expound like Moses from God's mouth, but Reish Lakish said it was not original, it was a baraita from Torat Kohanim. Rabbi Yohanan then learned that whole work in three days and understood it in three months.

12.event: While Rabbi Yehuda and others sat before Rabbi Tarfon, a yevama came to perform halitza.
12.turn: Rabbi Tarfon instructed all present to respond 'He who had his shoe removed.'
12.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled sitting with others before Rabbi Tarfon when a widow came to perform the halitza ceremony. Rabbi Tarfon told everyone present to call out together, 'He who had his shoe removed.'
12.missing: Whether they did so or anything that followed; the incident is cited as a source for a practice.

13.event: Rabba bar Hiyya conducted a halitza with a non-leather slipper, alone, and at night.
13.turn: Shmuel criticized him for relying on individual minority opinions.
13.outcome: The act stood under Shmuel's sarcastic rebuke.
13.summary: Rabba bar Hiyya from Ctesiphon performed a halitza ceremony using a slipper, as the sole judge, and at night. Shmuel remarked sarcastically on how bold this master was to follow lone opinions in his practice.

14.actor: Mar Yehuda and Rav Huna bar Yehuda
14.event: Visiting Rav Huna bar Yehuda's house, Mar Yehuda saw people carrying among trees not planted in rows.
14.turn: He challenged Rav Huna for not following Avimi's view.
14.outcome: Rav Huna answered that he followed Rav Nahman, who permits it.
14.summary: Mar Yehuda visited the home of Rav Huna bar Yehuda and saw people carrying on Shabbat in an enclosure whose trees were not planted in rows. He asked whether Rav Huna did not accept Avimi's ruling forbidding this. Rav Huna replied that he followed Rav Nahman, who permitted it.

17.event: In Rabbi Pedat's house a beam so heavy it took ten people to lift was placed against the door to secure it.
17.turn: Rabbi Pedat said nothing against it.
17.outcome: He explained that it had the status of a utensil.
17.summary: In Rabbi Pedat's house there was a huge beam that took ten people to lift, and they would set it against the door to secure it. Rabbi Pedat never objected, explaining that the beam counted as a utensil and could be used this way on Shabbat.
17.missing: It describes a recurring practice rather than a single event with a turn.

18.actor: Rav Mordekhai (reporting) and a divorced woman
18.event: A bill of divorce lay closer to the woman than the husband and was lost.
18.outcome: They required her to undergo halitza.
18.summary: Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi of a case where a bill of divorce landed closer to a woman than to her husband but never reached her hand. When the husband died, the rabbis required her to undergo halitza because her divorce was in doubt.
18.missing: Names, circumstances and the course of the case; it is a bare report of a ruling.

19.event: A man walked past the door of his father-in-law's house.
19.turn: He was suspected of an affair with his mother-in-law.
19.summary: A certain man passed by the entrance of his father-in-law's house and Rav Sheshet had him lashed. The reason was that he was suspected of a relationship with his mother-in-law.
19.missing: Only a bare report of the incident, cited to resolve a legal question.

20.event: Rav Kahana, a priest, took a cloth as payment for a firstborn's redemption.
20.turn: He declared that to him the cloth was worth five sela.
20.outcome: The redemption was accepted with the cloth.
20.summary: Rav Kahana, a priest, accepted a cloth at a firstborn son's redemption ceremony, telling the father that to him the cloth was worth the required five sela. A related report tells that Mar bar Rav Ashi paid thirteen dinars for a cloth worth ten.
20.missing: Little beyond the act and statement; both incidents are cited as legal precedents.
